title: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Mollusc shell pigment patterns are generated like one-dimensional cellular automata

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells are produced line by line by pigment-secreting elements whose new states depend on neighbors' previous states, so the range of shell patterns closely matches the patterns of the simplest symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: comparing the patterns in these pictures with patterns on actual mollusc shells, one notices the remarkable fact that the range of patterns that occur in the two cases is extremely similar.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Biological Pigmentation Patterns” (from p. 422), p. 425. Scope: pigmentation patterns on mollusc shells

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-26: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Pattern comparison and local transition inference are feasible for suitably imaged shells, and CA outputs are readily available. Current public morphology data are not a curated developmental time series, and rival local models can generate similar motifs. The phenomenological match is more resolvable than the cellular mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Extract growth-line-resolved shell pigmentation, infer local transition dependencies, and compare held-out predictive likelihood and pattern-space coverage for symmetric one-dimensional cellular automata versus reaction-diffusion and nonlocal models. Local neighbor dependence plus superior CA prediction would support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public shell images undersample pattern diversity and may lack calibrated growth orientation.

Static shells provide outcomes but not direct states of pigment-secreting cells.

Visual similarity has weak mechanism discrimination.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.58
operationalizability: 0.68
data adequacy: 0.4
data existence: 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Because the shell stores successive rows, local determinism can be tested by rule inference rather than by a glance at resemblance. Public images and the finite list of symmetric elementary rules make that comparison feasible for a substantial sample. Physiology that would confirm neighbor-to-neighbor secretion is mostly missing, so the mechanism remains less resolved than the geometric range.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Treat each shell pattern as a space-time record and test whether a symmetrical nearest-neighbor two-color rule reproduces it, then compare the set of successful rules with the set of patterns on real shells. A close match of the two ranges would support the claim; many common shell patterns that require longer-range or multi-state rules, or a physiological map that is not a local neighbor rule, would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The pigment physiology of the mantle edge is rarely measured, so rule inference from the shell is a proxy for the mechanism.

A similar range of pictures can be produced by reaction-diffusion models that are not cellular automata.

fields.value:
